title: Three Observations on NSC Fall 2026 Enrollment Data
author: Phil Hill
summary: Phil Hill challenges the media framing of the National Student Clearinghouse's preliminary fall 2026 data, which reported undergraduate enrollment as holding steady at plus 0.6 percent. His read is that 2026 marks the transition from post-pandemic recovery to renewed enrollment decline, regardless of whether this fall finishes slightly positive or negative. He supports this with three observations. First, undergraduate enrollment moves in multi-year trends, and the growth rate is crossing from positive to negative. Second, the demographic cliff argument, though sometimes overstated, is real, with domestic 18-year-old graduates declining from 2025/26 through roughly 2039 as a delayed effect of the Great Recession birth drop. Third, the gains come from dual enrollment, up 3.9 percent, which roughly equals the entire net gain, and which pulls students forward rather than adding new undergraduates. He urges institutions to keep improving retention and adult access but to base enrollment assumptions on a recovery that is running out of momentum.
points: The headline of steady enrollment hides a trend in which growth rates are falling and crossing into decline around this year.
Domestic 18-year-old high school graduates peaked in 2025 and are projected to decline into 2039, driven by births that fell after 2008.
Dual enrollment growth of about 120,000 students roughly accounts for the entire 100,000 net undergraduate gain, so without it enrollment would already be falling.
Dual enrollment is a pull-forward effect, because those students are already counted and will not appear as new undergraduates later.
Institutions should keep improving retention and access but plan budgets around a weakening recovery.
quotes: The coverage reports the slowdown. The larger question is what that slowdown marks. Taking a broader look at trends and looking at age composition shows some different headlines.
The decline in childbirths began with the Great Recession in roughly 2008, and 18 years later, here we are.

Adult student populations, increases in immediate college enrollments, and better retention rates can offset these numbers, but absent a massive change in those numbers, they can only dampen the impacts of the decline.
High school dual enrollment, roughly captured by NSC as those 17 years or younger, increased yet again, by 3.9%. No other age group came close.

Without dual enrollment gains, total undergraduate enrollments would already be in decline. And keep in mind that dual enrollment is a pull-forward effect—these students will not be new undergraduates when they graduate; they are already in the numbers.
But they should build their enrollment assumptions around a recovery that is running out of momentum. Finishing slightly above zero in Fall 2026 would offer little reassurance about the years ahead.
My read is that 2026 marks the transition from the post-pandemic recovery toward renewed enrollment decline.
